2: (a) Most candidates recognised that a limited company had limited liability or could sell shares. Stronger responses were able to provide a precise definition. A common mistake was to define other terms such as a private limited company, public limited company, or private sector business. Others made vague statements about ‘not losing assets’ which could not be awarded. (b) This question was answered well by most candidates. The best responses included having a target and motivating employees. A common mistake was to repeat a similar point for both answers which can only be awarded once. (c) Most responses included good knowledge for this question. A common mistake was to repeat the same point of application for each answer. For example, instead of using shoes each time, responses could have mentioned the business made 18000 pairs each week. (d) Most candidates were able to gain knowledge marks for recognising employees might want higher wages and suppliers may want to charge higher prices. However most struggled to analyse why these stakeholder objectives might create a conflict with GBR’s own objective. Many responses identified lower profit without explaining why this may happen. For example, higher wages could result in higher costs, and it is the higher costs which could lower profit. 3: (a) This question was answered well. A common mistake was to repeat similar points, using different words. For example, earning money and pay for basic needs are alternative ways of expressing the same idea, and will only be awarded once. (b) Most responses either identified a trade union was a group formed of workers or it was an organisation that existed to protect rights. Stronger responses were able to provide a precise definition. A common mistake was to confuse the term with a pressure group. (c) Most candidates gained at least one knowledge mark for identifying growth. The strongest answers gained full marks for identifying all four stages of the business cycle. A common mistake was to confuse the term with product life cycle. Others identified the factors of production. (d) This question produced a range of responses. Stronger responses explained how induction training allowed new employees to become familiar with the workplace leading to fewer mistakes. Application marks were often awarded for recognising this was a hotel and had 20 employees. Most responses struggled to explain possible limitations. Some responses recognised it could be time consuming or increase cost but were not able to develop this into analysis. A common mistake was to confuse the method with on-the-job or off-the-job training. Others discussed general reasons why training was necessary. 4: (a) Most answers lacked the necessary precision needed to gain both marks for this question. Some responses understood niche market represented a smaller segment of a market but were unable to provide a full definition. There were vague statements about the size of the market or assumptions made about the product such as it must be high-quality or have a high price. Others confused niche market with market segmentation. (b) This question was poorly answered by most candidates. Stronger responses identified points such as ‘avoid misleading advertising’ however, responses did not develop to identify a second impact. A common mistake was to discuss other areas of legal control concerning the environment or employment. Some responses confused legal controls with tariffs and quotas. Others repeated similar points for both impacts which can only be awarded once. (c) This question was answered well by most candidates who understood a good brand image could help increase customers or provide opportunities to charge higher prices. There was good application for this question as responses recognised this was a new business or that it made furniture. A common mistake was to forget to use different points of application to link each answer to the context, which meant responses could not be awarded the second application mark.
